Summary of Study:
Yuan and colleagues conduct a numerical modeling study where they couple geodynamic (ASPECT), landscape evolution (FastScape), and orographic rainfall (LFPM 1.0) models to explore the dynamics and co-evolution of deformation, erosion, and precipitation during convergent orogenesis. Motivated by the ambiguity of past studies aiming to test the exciting hypothesis of tectonic-climate-erosion coupling and feedbacks. This study conducts three general experiments (high, intermediate, and low landscape erodibility) designed to span a range of conditions in natural orogens. In these experiments, relevant parameters are tracked in space and time (e.g., strain, erosion, exhumation, elevation, precipitation), and correlations between uplift, erosion, and precipitation rate are tracked. The results show distinct behaviors among the different models, where low erodibility models show weak correlations between these parameters, and as erodibility increases, uplift, erosion, and precipitation rates are more strongly correlated. Within the context of previous work by Wolf et al. (2022), the increasing correlation is associated with the transition from a strength-limited to erosion-limited orogenic system defined by the non-dimensional “Beaumont number”.
The results are argued to demonstrate systems where tectonic-climate-erosion feedbacks are strong (erosion-limited case) and where they are expected to be weak (strength-limited case), and natural example orogens that might meet these conditions are noted. The authors emphasize the importance of results from the intermediate erodibility case in an attempt to reconcile contradictory interpretations of tectonic-climate-erosion coupling, or lack thereof, in the Himalayas, a setting where the debate over these feedbacks has been active for decades. The authors demonstrate that the intermediate erodibility models transition between erosion- and strength-limited as new faults propagate outward through time. There are transient periods where the windward flank of the modeled orogen is locally in steady state, and climate appears to “control erosion”. Other times, when a new thrust breaks, the system is perturbed, and tectonics locally “controls erosion” and surface uplift before orography catches up and temporarily slows thrust propagation, and a local steady-state is once again achieved. This cycle (climate-moduled inch-worm orogenesis?) is argued to help explain apparently contradictory results in the Himalayas, where some locations are in the steady-state phase while others are in the thrust-propagation phase of the intermediate erodibility orogenic cycle.
Major Comments and Recommendations:
This is an impressive study. The technical achievement of the model coupling is eye-catching and of broad interest. The results are exciting, building upon the excellent work of Wolf et al. (2022) with new and creative insights. This work will be of interest to a wide range of earth scientists, making it well-suited for the broad readership of Nature Communications. The modeling presented improves understanding of how earth surface processes (via erodibility) and climate can impact convergent orogensis. An important element of the study is the sensitivity of the system to climate (more precisely here, orographic rainfall), at least as parameterized in the models used here, is a function of “bulk landscape erodiblity” and characteristics of tectonics (i.e., convergence velocity, crustal strength). The study provides important insight into where we might or might not expect to see systems with tectonic-climate-erosion coupling and feedbacks.
I have a few comments and questions the authors might consider in revision. I’ve broken these out into “major comments” which I provide in this section and line-by-line comments below.
(1) The manuscript abstract and intro promise to address tectonic vs. climate controls on erosion. With the sophisticated modeling approach, it seems like it should be possible to quantify the relative strengths of tectonic vs climate in modulating topographic growth, strain localization, and erosional focusing, specifically along the windward thrust front. I assume a modified Beaumont number could encapsulate this by including precipitation in the erodibility calculation and only focusing on the windward part of the model domain (provided it makes sense to do so). If it is easy to come up with a parameter like this, it could be tracked through time and used to show how the relative importance of orographic rainfall changes through time in the intermediate erodibility models. Furthermore, I mention this because I wasn’t convinced that the correlations between U & E and P & E fully demonstrated tectonics vs. climate, and I’m not sure this is a well-posed question. I’m not criticizing the authors; the community has rallied around this “question” for better or worse, even though it is not clearly testable. Tectonic, climate, and surface processes all drive the dynamics of the orogenic system, as elegantly shown in this work, and therefore, I don’t think one can easily test for “climate vs tectonics”. A more precise question is the relative strength of climate and tectonic (and surface) processes in strain and erosion localization in a tectonically active system. So, from these model results, I am wondering if it is possible to quantify the relative strength of tectonics and climate in localizing strain and erosion. I hope this is possible with these models because then we can design field experiments to measure relevant quantities and test these ideas in natural systems.

Beyond these three comments, I have some comments, questions, and suggested revisions below. Despite my few criticisms, I think this is a great study. The model coupling is impressive, as are the experiments and scientific insights. Importantly, my comments don’t require additional model runs, but only perhaps some relatively minor analysis of the existing model outputs and some small tweaks to the text.
Great work!
All the best,
- Sean F. Gallen

### Reviewer 2

Coordination between deformation, precipitation, and erosion during orogenic growth is a good paper that extends the state of the art on modeling the coupled climate/surface/processes/tectonics of active orogens. The writing is clear, the methods and results are comprehensively explained, given the short format (note the generous additional materials) and the problem is something that has long been of interest in the community.
The modelling seems like a pretty clear incremental improvement on the prior work by some of the authors (thinking here of the 2022 Nature paper Topography of mountain belts controlled by rheology and surface processes) and many others, with new rheological and climate models, although it should of course be noted that coupled orographic/surface process/geodynamic modelling has a long tradition.
It’s not very clear that the high correlations between rock uplift and erosion and precipitation and erosion, are especially important, beyond what the authors note (“The strong correlations indicate that the orogen has reached a high degree of steady state”). The modeling is consistent with these orogens being close to steady state. High correlations are expected in this case as erosion matches uplift, and since most of the erosion is stream power driven in the model, we expect, and observe, a high but slightly lower correlation for precipitation and uplift as well (with diffusive/landslide processes explaining the rest of the relief lowering).
I very much disagree that “Our modeling results can resolve the major debate about whether tectonics or climate controls erosion in large orogens” (257). In the first place, modeling alone can’t resolve this debate. In the second place, this study is an incremental improvement on previous coupled models, so if this paper was capable of resolving this debate, these prior works would’ve resolved it before this paper was written. And finally, a critic might claim that the surface process and climate models present are insufficient to make firm claims.
This goes beyond the fact that the stream power laws themselves remain empirically undemonstrated (although they clearly create appropriate dendritic landscapes) despite their ubiquity in numerical modeling studies. To state the obvious, the current climate and surface process conditions of the orogens investigated here are not the typical or average climate conditions at the Myr scale.
For most of the relevant period, most of these mountain ranges have been glaciated. Not only were the temperatures lower everywhere, wind direction and precipitation patterns varied by location. Heavily glaciated mountain ranges are not fluvially (and thus stream-powered model related) eroded, they are glacially eroded. It could be argued that erosion correlates with total water flow, be it solid or liquid, but at a minimum stream power would not be the right framing and sub-glacial temperatures (especially whether the ice is frozen at the bed) is very important. Furthermore, if orogenic precipitation is very important (and so having a sophisticated orographic model is important), then shifting climate patterns are also highly relevant, and using current wind and precipitation patterns are also, on average, quite different. Although not present in the paper’s model, other workers have focused on threshold effects with fluvial erosion, in which case even changes in the pattern of precipitation events (to or from extreme events dominating the precipitation load) could be significant. At a minimum, the cold air of the quaternary contained less moisture which, on average, reduces precipitation (which is falling as snow).

HIGH-LEVEL COMMENTS
In this manuscript, the authors report a series of experiments with a coupled numerical model of mountain chain formation by plate collision, erosion (and deposition), and orographic precipitation. The study uses the model to examine the degree of correlation between rock uplift rate, erosion rate, and precipitation rate, and how this varies dynamically during different stages in process of generating new thrusts at the margins of the orogen. The experiments, which are beautifully illustrated with colour images as well as animation in the supplemental material, provide insight into the dynamic nature of orogenesis, and the transient cycles that arise around the creation of each new outer thrust. They also illustrate the potential influence of erosional efficiency on orogen form and scale.
The computational effort behind these experiments is surely substantial. I don't know whether the software engineering to couple ASPECT, FastScape, and the orographic precipitation model was undertaken specifically for this study or had been done previously for other work, but in any event it seems like a major technical achievement. Other studies have reported coupled deformation and erosion models, but this is the first I have seen that uses this particular combination of models.
Regarding the significance of the problem addressed: The possibility of a dynamic feedback between mountain building and precipitation climatology has been an exciting but unproven hypothesis going back at least 30 years. Investigators have tested for correlations between quantities like tectonic motion rates, precipitation rates, and denudation rates. One barrier has been in interpreting the meaning of such correlations (or lack of correlations). To do so arguably requires a mechanistic theoretical framework, and that's part of what this paper contributes. Although numerical modeling that integrates theory for crustal strain, orographic precipitation, erosion, sediment transport, and sediment deposition has been done before, one thing I have not seen previously is examination of statistical correlations between tectonic, precipitation, and erosion rates under different scenarios. These correlations are among the things one can actually measure in the field, and the model provides a framework with which to ask what those correlations ought to look like.
One of the interesting findings is that stages of transience, when a new thrust fault (or shear zone) is forming at the margin of a growing orogen, can effectively interrupt an otherwise strong correlation between tectonics, precipitation, and erosion, even though a dynamic feedback is still operating. Because this is a numerical model, we know already that the processes of deformation, precipitation, and erosion are tightly coupled, so the novelty lies in asking how that coupling would manifest in the kinds of data that we can actually collect from real orogens. The finding implies that lack of correlation among rates of tectonic motion, erosion, and precipitation could just be symptoms of transient adjustment, rather than a lack of dynamic coupling.
A comment about framing: The central concern of the paper is stated in the abstract as 'whether tectonics or climate controls erosion in active orogens is much debated.' With all due respect, this phrasing, which appears repeatedly in the manuscript, is imprecise and could be framed more clearly. The following is going to sound like picking on language rather than the technical substance of the manuscript (which it is), but I believe language matters. In this particular case, the authors are following in a long tradition of describing orogens as being 'controlled' (or alternatively, 'driven') either by tectonics or climate. The either-or phrasing implies that only one of those two things - tectonics or climate - can 'control' erosion in an active orogen. But it seems undeniable that both should influence a convergent orogen. After all, erosion would not occur on a planet without a climate system (or at least not in ways it happens on earth). And without tectonics, you wouldn't have an orogen to erode in the first place. In that sense, erosion on earth requires both climate and tectonics, and answer to the question 'are orogens controlled by tectonics or climate?' must surely be 'yes'!
I think what the authors are really asking is something more nuanced, maybe something more along the lines of: given the natural range of plate convergence rates and precipitation rates on planet earth, do the morphology and erosion rates/patterns in a convergent orogen tend to be more sensitive to changes in convergence rate or to equivalent changes (relative to their natural range) in advective moisture flux? In other words, the 'tectonics versus climate' question can be made more precise and therefore more useful by framing it in terms of changes in a rate normalized by a natural range in rates.
Alternatively, maybe the key question is more along the lines of: under what conditions would the orientation of atmospheric moisture flux across an orogen have the most (or least) influence on the orogen evolution, and why? The results obviously speak to this. Contrary to the findings of previous, simpler models, they find that a smaller, equilibrated orogen will tend to be less sensitive to moisture source direction, whereas a larger, transient-growth orogen will to tend to be more sensitive. If this is the main intended focus, I would love to see the authors say more about why. To what extent does the difference in sensitivity arise from orogen size (the low-erodibility case producing MUCH bigger orogens, which therefore produce a bigger orographic effect on precipitation), as opposed to orogen age or stage of evolution?
Whatever the case, I recommend adding text to the paper that articulates a more precise version of the tectonics-versus-climate question. Framing the question in a way that could be clearly answered with the right data would be in the spirit of one of the key strengths of the paper, which is that it makes predictions about things one can actually measure. (While we are on the topic of wording, I appreciate the use of the word 'coordinate' in the title, because it conveys a sense of dynamic interaction.)
Experimental setup: The experiments are run for a fixed duration of 50 million years. That is a reasonable choice, but if I understand correctly, it means that two out of the three main experiments reported in the manuscript are in a state of transient growth, while the other has reached dynamic equilibrium between convergence flux and erosional flux. To what extent, if any, do the conclusions rest on this choice of run time? For example, if the models had been run for only 1 million years, would the high erodibility case also show transient de-correlation between rock uplift and erosion rates? Or if they had been run to 100 my, would the other two cases reach a quasi-equilibrium, and if so would they still produce cycles of thrust birth? Or is it less a question of time than of orogen width, with transient thrust growth only being significant when the orogen is wider than N crustal thicknesses (or whatever the relevant length scale is)? It would be great to see some discussion of these issues in the text. It is an important issue because it relates to the generalizability of the results. For example, are the cycles of thrust birth restricted to the initial transient stage of the orogen, and therefore not expected for an orogen that has reached dynamic equilibrium ('steady state')? Or, as the high-erodibility movies suggest, should we expect perpetual cycles of thrust birth and growth on the side of the subducting plate?
